findings.claim: Equatorial Guinea: "life expectancy sits below 60 and most live in poverty".
findings.truth: Life expectancy at birth in Equatorial Guinea was 63.7 years in 2023 (62.1 in 2020), so it has not been below 60 for the years a current student would quote. The wider point (high GDP, poor social outcomes) stands, because the high-income average is about 80.
findings.evidence: World Bank SP.DYN.LE00.IN, Equatorial Guinea and High income, 2020-2023

findings.truth: Same error as F1; the figure is about 63.

findings.claim: "In sub-Saharan Africa, around 27 babies in every 1,000 die before their first birthday — ten times the rate in HICs."
findings.truth: Sub-Saharan Africa's infant mortality rate was 48.2 per 1,000 live births in 2023. 27 is close to the WORLD average, not the sub-Saharan African one. With 48 the "ten times" comparison is correct (high income = 4.3 per 1,000); with 27 it is not.
findings.evidence: World Bank SP.DYN.IMRT.IN, Sub-Saharan Africa 48.2 (2023) and High income 4.3 (2023)

findings.claim: "UN Sustainable Development Goal 3 targets a global infant mortality rate of 12 per 1,000 by 2030."
findings.truth: SDG target 3.2 sets NEONATAL mortality at 12 per 1,000 live births and under-5 mortality at 25 per 1,000 live births by 2030. There is no SDG infant (under-1) mortality target of 12.

findings.claim: Flashcard [12] answer: "Goal 3 (SDG 3), aiming to cut infant mortality to 12 per 1,000 by 2030."
findings.truth: Same error as F4; the 12 per 1,000 target is for newborn (neonatal) deaths.

findings.claim: "the GAVI alliance now reaches more than half of the world's children" — repeated in knowledge check [3] and flashcard [7].
findings.truth: Gavi's own statement is that it supports the immunisation of almost half the world's children, not more than half.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, GAVI: "Gavi supports the immunization of almost half the world's children"

findings.claim: "oral rehydration salts for diarrhoea, the second-biggest killer of under-fives" — repeated in practice question [1] mark scheme and flashcard [9].
findings.truth: WHO now ranks diarrhoeal disease as the THIRD leading cause of death in children aged 1-59 months (about 443,832 under-5 deaths a year). The older "second" ranking is out of date.

findings.claim: Mark scheme for "Explain how social challenges in sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia are being tackled" offers "Bolsa Família conditional cash transfers" as an acceptable named example.
findings.truth: Bolsa Família is Brazilian. The question restricts the answer to sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia, so a student who follows this key would write about the wrong region and gain no credit. India's school meals scheme is a true in-region equivalent.
findings.evidence: Spec Theme 7 key idea 7.2 (sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia); question wording

findings.claim: "in countries like Niger and Chad, only around half of girls complete primary school".
findings.truth: Female primary completion is 44.8% in Niger (2023) and 36.3% in Chad (2021), so "fewer than half" is accurate and "around half" overstates it.
findings.evidence: World Bank SE.PRM.CMPT.FE.ZS, Niger and Chad

findings.claim: "a kilo of beef takes 25 times the water of a kilo of grain" — repeated in flashcard [12].
findings.truth: Global average water footprints are 15,415 L/kg for beef against 1,608 L/kg for wheat bread, 1,222 for maize and 2,497 for rice: a ratio of roughly six to thirteen times, so "around ten times" is the defensible figure.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Water footprint (Mekonnen & Hoekstra global averages)

findings.claim: "The UN estimates every £1 spent on restoration returns up to £30 in benefits over time."
findings.truth: The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration figure is in US dollars: every US$1 invested in restoration creates up to US$30 in economic benefits. The currency was changed without converting the value.
findings.evidence: UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration / UNEP headline figure

findings.claim: "Cranes returned to breed in the area in 2007 after a 400-year absence" (Great Fen) — repeated in flashcard [3], which pins the event to the Great Fen itself.
findings.truth: The 2007 crane breeding widely reported in the Fens was at Lakenheath Fen in Suffolk, not at the Great Fen. Wikipedia's Great Fen Project article records no cranes, and its Common crane article attaches the "over 400 years" phrase to a 2016 hatching in Wales. Options: (a) soften to "cranes have returned to breed in the Fens after centuries away" and drop the 2007 date and the Great Fen attribution; (b) leave it if Tom can confirm a Great Fen breeding record for 2007 from the Wildlife Trust BCN. I could not settle it from an allowed source, so no edit is written.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Great Fen Project; Wikipedia, Common crane
findings.ruling: Leave: unverified this session (crane record / Green Tax rate).

findings.claim: "The Maldives charges a Green Tax of US$6 per night" — repeated in flashcard [8].
findings.truth: The Maldives Green Tax is understood to have doubled from 1 January 2025, to US$12 per person per night at resorts, hotels and liveaboard vessels, with US$6 kept for guesthouses of 50 rooms or fewer. That would make the flat US$6 statement out of date. Wikipedia carries no Green Tax entry and the Maldives tax authority is outside the permitted fetch list, so I could not confirm the new rate. Options: (a) update to "US$12 per night at resorts and hotels, US$6 at small guesthouses"; (b) drop the figure and keep "a nightly Green Tax". I recommend (b) unless Tom checks the rate.
findings.evidence: no permitted source available; flagged for checking
findings.ruling: Leave: unverified this session (crane record / Green Tax rate).

findings.claim: "Roughly 160 million children worldwide work in jobs that should be done by adults" — repeated in flashcard [4].
findings.truth: 160 million is the ILO/UNICEF estimate for 2020. The ILO's 2024 round reports a lower figure (about 138 million). The ILO page returned 404 on fetch, so the number is left alone; 160 million is still the figure in most GCSE textbooks and would not cost a mark.
findings.evidence: ILO/UNICEF Global Estimates 2020 (fetch of the 2024 release failed)

findings.claim: "Sub-Saharan Africa hosts more than 7 million refugees and asylum seekers".
findings.truth: True but understated: UNHCR now puts the regional total nearer 9 million. "More than 7 million" is not wrong, so no edit.

findings.claim: "more than 60 million tonnes of e-waste a year — the equivalent of 350 cruise ships".
findings.truth: The tonnage is right (62 million tonnes in 2022). The 350-cruise-ships comparison belongs to the older 53.6 million tonne figure, so the image now understates the mass. Not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Electronic waste (62 Mt in 2022); Global E-waste Monitor 2020 analogy

findings.claim: "The UK has lost roughly 90% of its wetlands since 1700" — repeated in the knowledge check stem and flashcard [1].
findings.truth: The 90% loss figure is real but is usually quoted over the last 100 years rather than since 1700. The date is not settled enough to change, and the percentage is correct.

summary: Four lessons checked; 17 findings, 11 of them fixed by 16 edits. The two that would cost marks are both in lesson 2: sub-Saharan Africa's infant mortality is given as 27 per 1,000 when the true figure is 48 (27 is the world average), and SDG 3's 12-per-1,000 target is described as an infant mortality target when it is a neonatal one. Exam framing is clean: no lesson names the board, claims both Theme 7 and Theme 8 are compulsory, invents examiner comments or uses impossible marks, and the one extended label found reads "8 marks plus SPaG", which matches the 84 plus 4 SPaG paper.
